children: By Daniel Wiessner

A National Labor Relations Board official has ruled that student residential advisers at Stanford University are the school's employees and can vote on whether to join a union, teeing up review by the board on the novel issue.

Regional Director Christy Kwon in Oakland said in the decision released on Saturday that more than 430 "residential student leaders" perform services under the control of Stanford for which they are compensated, making them employees under federal labor law.

Stanford had argued that being a residential adviser is part of a student's educational experience and primarily benefits their education, putting them beyond the reach of the law. But Kwon said that claim ignored the high degree of control Stanford has over the students, the $12,400 stipend they receive each year, and the fact that they do not receive academic credit.

The labor board in a 2016 decision involving Columbia University held that graduate students who teach courses as part of their degree work are employees who can join unions. Today, nearly 40% of such students are represented by unions, according to research by Hunter College in New York City.
Kwon in her decision said the same test adopted by the board in the Columbia case should apply to residential advisers. She said she would set a date for the election after consulting the parties.
A spokesperson for Stanford said the decision was being reviewed.

Residential Assistants United Rising, the union that sought the election, in a statement said its organizing campaign began last year in the face of the rising cost of living, reduced RA positions and stipends that do not fully cover the costs of housing and food.
"During this coming election, we hope to reiterate what we have proven these last 13 months: that RAs deserve the dignity of union recognition," the union said.

Residential advisers at a handful of schools including Barnard College in New York City and Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania have unionized over the last few years, but in those cases the schools either voluntarily recognized the unions or did not argue that RAs were not their employees.

An NLRB regional director in 2017 held that RAs at George Washington University in Washington, D.C., were the school's employees and ordered a union election for them. But the union withdrew its petition the day before the vote, scuttling a chance for an incoming Republican NLRB majority to rule that resident advisers are not schools' employees.
Some unions similarly withdrew petitions involving student-athletes or teaching assistants in expectation that NLRB members appointed by President Donald Trump would rule against them.

The board regained a Democratic majority in 2021 under former President Joe Biden, but Republicans now have a 3-1 edge and are expected to roll back a series of Biden-era decisions widely seen as favoring unions.
The case is Stanford University, National Labor Relations Board, No. 32-RC-386778.
